---
title: "Getting started with RSiena"
author: "Tom A.B. Snijders"
description: >
  A first analysis with RSiena: make the data, specify a model,
  estimate it, check convergence, and test parameters.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# RSiena writes report files to the working directory; keep them out of the site.
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = tempdir())
```

This article shows a basic sequence of commands for estimating a
Stochastic Actor-oriented Model (SAOM) with RSiena.
It is based on the script `basic_RSiena.Rmd` by Tom Snijders
(see [the scripts catalogue](https://github.com/stocnet/rsiena/issues/4)),
updated to the function names that RSiena uses since version 1.6.0.

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(RSiena)
```

## The data

We use the `s50` data that come with the package:
an excerpt of 50 pupils from the Teenage Friends and Lifestyle Study,
with friendship networks at three waves,
and the alcohol use and smoking of each pupil at each wave.
See `?s50` for a description.

```{r data}
dim(s501)
s501[1:6, 1:10]
head(s50a)
```

If you have your own data in files, read them as matrices,
for example with `as.matrix(read.table("network1.dat"))`,
and continue in the same way.

## Roles of the variables

Each variable in a SIENA analysis has a role.
The **dependent variables** are the variables whose change the model explains.
Here the dependent variable is the friendship network.
First make a 50 × 50 × 3 array of the three adjacency matrices,
and then give it the role of a dependent variable:

```{r depvar}
friendship <- as_dependent_rsiena(array(c(s501, s502, s503),
                                        dim = c(50, 50, 3)))
friendship
```

The **covariates** are explanatory variables.
We use smoking at wave 1 as a constant actor covariate,
and alcohol use as a changing actor covariate:

```{r covariates}
smoke1  <- as_covariate_rsiena(s50s[, 1])
alcohol <- as_covariate_rsiena(s50a)
```

(Only the first wave of smoking is used here,
to show a constant covariate.)

Then put the variables together in one data object:

```{r makedata}
mydata <- make_data_rsiena(friendship, smoke1, alcohol)
mydata
```

`write_report(mydata)` writes a file with basic descriptive statistics
of the data to the working directory.
Read it before you estimate a model:
it shows, for example, the density, the number of changes between waves,
and the Jaccard index, which tells whether there is enough stability
between waves for a SAOM.

```{r report, results = "hide"}
write_report(mydata)
```

## Specifying the model

The model specification is an *effects object*.
`make_specification()` makes one that holds all the effects
that are possible for this data, with a few basic effects included:

```{r effects}
myeff <- make_specification(mydata)
myeff
```

`effectsDocumentation(myeff)` gives a table of all the available effects.
Chapter 12 of the [RSiena manual](https://github.com/stocnet/rsiena/releases/latest/download/RSiena_Manual.pdf)
describes each effect.
Add structural effects for network closure,
and effects of the covariates:
the sender (ego), receiver (alter), and similarity effects of alcohol,
and the similarity effect of smoking.

```{r specify}
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, list(transTrip, cycle3))
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, list(egoX, altX, simX), covar1 = "alcohol")
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, simX, covar1 = "smoke1")
myeff
```

## Estimating the model

The algorithm has many settings,
but the defaults are usually good.
Set the random seed, so that you get the same results each time:

```{r algorithm}
myalgo <- set_algorithm_saom(seed = 435123)
```

`siena()` estimates the parameters.
`batch = TRUE` writes short progress information to the console
instead of opening a window.

```{r estimate}
ans <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff, control_algo = myalgo, batch = TRUE)
ans
```

### Convergence

Before you interpret the estimates, check the convergence of the algorithm.
All convergence t-ratios should be less than 0.1 in absolute value,
and the overall maximum convergence ratio should be less than 0.25:

```{r convergence}
ans$tconv.max
```

If the convergence is not good enough, estimate again
from the previous result, with `prevAns`:

```{r prevans, eval = FALSE}
ans <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff, control_algo = myalgo,
             prevAns = ans, batch = TRUE)
```

`summary(ans)` gives more details,
and the output file in the working directory gives the most details.

## Adding an effect

Add the transitive reciprocated triplets effect,
which is an interaction between transitivity and reciprocity,
and estimate again.
Because the new model only adds an effect,
the estimation can start from the previous result:

```{r add}
myeff <- set_effect(myeff, transRecTrip)
ans1 <- siena(mydata, effects = myeff, control_algo = myalgo,
              prevAns = ans, batch = TRUE)
ans1
```

## Testing parameters

To test a parameter, divide the estimate by its standard error,
and compare the result with a standard normal distribution
(with a critical value of about 2).
`test_parameter()` does this.
The parameters are numbered as in the table above
(the rate parameters are not counted).
For example, the test of alcohol similarity:

```{r test1}
alcsim <- which(ans1$effects$shortName == "simX" &
                ans1$effects$interaction1 == "alcohol")
test_parameter(ans1, tested = alcsim)
```

A joint test of the three alcohol effects:

```{r test3}
alc <- which(ans1$effects$interaction1 == "alcohol" &
             ans1$effects$type == "eval")
test_parameter(ans1, tested = alc)
```

A single effect can be significant while a joint test of several effects
is not, because the other effects add little to the model.

  to study selection and influence together:
  see [Co-evolution of networks and behaviour](coevolution.html).
- For more about model specification, estimation,
  and the tests that are available:
  see [Specifying and estimating a model](model-estimation.html).

## Try it yourself

1. Drop the effect of smoking similarity,
   with `set_effect(..., include = FALSE)`,
   and estimate the model again.
   Give the new effects object and the new results new names,
   so that you can compare the two models.
2. Replace the three effects of alcohol with the single effect
   of alcohol similarity, and estimate again.
